title: A grieving lighthouse keeper must decide whether to forfeit her beacon — and humanity’s safety — to sea creatures who promise the return of her drowned husband
content:
# The Hundred and Twenty-Seventh Step

The skiff’s outboard coughs awake on the third yank, blue smoke momentarily sweeter than the diesel-and-kelp stink that clings to the dock pilings. Mara Byrne doesn’t notice the tremor in her wrist; she counts—one Mississippi, two Mississippi—measuring the gap between ignition and steady thrum the way her husband once counted lightning. When the engine settles into its single-cylinder heartbeat she eases the throttle, letting the boat slide backwards over its own reflection so the lighthouse fractures and reforms in the black water. Forty-eight days left on the contract, she thinks, and the number tastes metallic, like the zinc that blooms overnight on brass.

Morning hasn’t arrived; the horizon is only a rumor of less dark. Overhead, gulls wheel in slow arcs, their wings creaking like wet leather, their calls thin enough to thread through the lattice of guy-wires that keep the tower upright against the Atlantic’s slow inhale. She smells them more than hears them—fish-rot and ozone, the smell of a world constantly remaking itself from salt and death. She keeps her eyes forward, on the lane between the island and the mainland that exists only in her head: red nun, green can, the invisible trench where Declan’s engine coughed once and died. The skiff’s fiberglass hull chatters across the swell, each slap a reminder that the sea is solid when it wants to be.

Breaker Point appears first as a bruise against the stars, then as a single sodium light above the cannery roof, then as the low silhouette she recognizes by the way it seems to hunch against weather. The town exhales fried herring and woodsmoke, nets drying on pilings and the sweet ghost of rum that lingers in every dock plank. She throttles down, letting the current take her the last hundred yards while she wipes salt spray from her lashes—blinks that rasp like fine sandpaper—and rehearses the lie she will tell Ezra: Supplies holding, weather fair, log uneventful. The truth is she has started talking to the empty cottage, that yesterday she found Daniel’s coffee mug on the workbench though she packed it away in March, that the beacon’s brass refuses to stay bright no matter how she polishes. But Ezra is mainland, and mainland deals in invoices, not hauntings.

The harbormaster’s float bumps her knee. She ties off with a rolling hitch, the rope cold enough to steal heat through her palm, and climbs the ladder that shudders under her weight. Her boots leave wet prints on the dock boards, each footprint collapsing as if the wood wants to erase her. The town sleeps except for St. Jude’s spire clock tolling once—five-thirty—its bronze voice shivering the air, the same note that tolled for Declan when the boat was three days overdue. She walks past the ice machine’s steady drip, past the co-op bulletin board papered with faded Polaroids of lost stern-men, past the chandlery door where someone has chalked the daily price of diesel in handwriting that gets shakier every week. Her reflection in the window is a ghost wearing her face: orange flotation suit unzipped to the sternum, hair yanked back with a bit of old fishing line, eyes ringed by fatigue that no longer expects rest.

Inside, Ezra counts fuses like rosary beads, lips moving silently. The shop smells of paraffin and mouse droppings, of coffee scorched to the pot’s bottom. He doesn’t look up when the bell jingles; he slides the cardboard box across the counter—oatmeal, rice, two tins of peaches, a pint of dark rum for the lighthouse log. The rum is tradition, the peaches contingency, the rice penance. She signs the requisition with the pen chained to the counter, ink blobbing where the ballpoint catches on rust.

“Fog’s riding two fathoms deep,” Ezra says, the closest anyone here will come to asking if she’s all right. Through the window she sees it: a pale wall advancing from the horizon, erasing first the channel markers, then the island, then the tower until only the beacon’s three quick flashes remain, strobing like a coded plea.

“Fog’s always early,” she answers, copper on her tongue. She tucks the check into her pocket—tuition money for Owen, sent anonymously because a son should not have to thank his mother for choosing lighthouse over funeral—and walks back into the dawn that still hasn’t broken. Behind her, the shop’s fluorescent light flickers once, twice, steadies, a heartbeat deciding whether to keep going.

At the dock edge she pauses, groceries in the skiff, hand on the piling. The fog has erased the lighthouse; she can’t even see the end of the breakwater. But she hears the beacon—three white flashes every thirty seconds—counted out by the automatic sensor she is paid to pretend still needs her. Somewhere inside that pale cloud the Fresnel lens is turning, throwing her reflection across twenty miles of black water, and for a moment she imagines the beam catching on something that has no business surfacing: a silhouette with Declan’s shoulders, Daniel’s height, a voice that knows her nickname but speaks with the sea’s mouth.

She starts the engine, throat raw with salt and unsaid things. The skiff pivots, points itself toward the invisible island, and accelerates into the fog that tastes of diesel, iodine, and something older—something that remembers every foot that ever touched it, every promise ever whispered into its damp and moving dark.

# Atmospheric Static

Chapter 2  

Mara scraped the final barnacle from the bronze valve and let the knife clatter onto the dock. Low tide still held the causeway dry, but the Atlantic leaned close, breathing through the planks in cold, diesel-laced exhalations. She wiped her hands on her jeans, leaving pale smears of salt and the iodine stink of torn kelp. Every knuckle throbbed—yesterday’s fog had settled into the joints and would stay until the next supply boat brought oranges, aspirin, and news of a land she no longer quite believed in.  

Gulls wheeled overhead, their cries thin as tearing paper. One dropped a mussel onto the granite ridge; the shell burst like a distant bulb popping. The bird tilted its head, judged, then screamed—only fragments, no meat. Mara knew the feeling.  

She straightened. The dock swayed beneath her boots, a slow see-saw that sent nausea up her spine. The motion was real—the Atlantic swelled ahead of the forecast storm—but the sickness was memory: Daniel steadying her the first time she’d stepped off his skiff onto this same plank walkway, his palm warm between her shoulder blades while the dock rolled. She still felt the ghost print, a heat that refused to cool nine weeks into widowhood.  

Inside the pump house the air turned still and metallic, thick with diesel that had sunk through the boards and never found its way out. The engine coughed once, twice, then settled into its arrhythmic mutter. She crouched, checked the fuel bowl—water beaded at the bottom like liquid mercury—and spotted, wedged in the brass petcock, a pinhead glow. Bioluminescent algae, or something smaller: a hatchling, translucent and dying in the air. Its light pulsed, weak as a night-light seen through fever.  

She pried it free with a fingernail, held it on her fingertip. The glow dimmed, flared—as if the creature knew her heat, her salt. Owen at six, pocketing fireflies in a jar lined with damp grass, crying when they stopped blinking. Light isn’t meant to be kept, she’d told him. She tipped the hatchling into the scupper. Tide sucked it away with a whisper.  

The engine hiccupped. She tightened the fuel line, wiped her hands, realized she was humming—low, under her breath—the shape-note hymn Daniel used to sing while coiling rope: Shenandoah. The tune felt smaller in her mouth, like a sweater washed too hot. She stopped.  

A gull landed on the roof peak, wings folding with the sound of wet laundry snapped in wind. It tilted one black eye, opened its bill, and Daniel’s voice emerged—not mimicry, not wind trick, but the exact cracked baritone that had once murmured her name against the hollow of her throat: “Mara.”  

She staggered, cracked her hip against the workbench. The gull screamed—ordinary seabird noise—and flapped away. The name hung, a condensation of breath and salt and something sweeter, like the ghost of the rum he’d drunk the night he died.  

She pressed her palms to her ears until blood roared. When she lowered them, only the engine’s heartless idle remained, and, farther off, surf inhaling against granite.  

On the bench sat Daniel’s coffee mug—oatmeal glaze, chipped rim—exactly where she swore she had not left it. The inside smelled of chicory and copper. She turned it over. A drop of coffee had dried on the bottom, a brown planet ringed by darker silt.  

Her throat tasted of rust. She set the mug down gentle as unexploded ordnance and stepped outside.  

The horizon had moved closer while she worked, a pewter wall climbing the sky like a tide turned on its side. The barometer in the kitchen window read 29.52 and falling. She felt the pressure in the roots of her teeth.  

She walked the dock anyway, needing the slap of water against pilings, needing proof that something still obeyed physics. Halfway to the tower the smell shifted—diesel fading beneath cold-water caves and iron ore, the breath of the Cut thirty fathoms off the eastern cliff. It rode the wind like warning, or invitation.  

The lighthouse stood ahead, white against purple cloud. At dusk the beacon would need striking—three white flashes every thirty seconds, a signature every trawler out of Breaker Point trusted more than the satellites that sometimes drifted here, confused by the trench’s iron heart. Ninety-eight-point-eight percent uptime: the clause that kept her employed, the promise that kept widows’ husbands off St. Jude’s memorial wall.  

She climbed the spiral, boots ringing on wrought-iron that vibrated with each Atlantic gust. Halfway up the air thinned, turned cold; her lungs filled with ground glass. She leaned against the curved wall. Salt sweat stung her eyes.  

Through the slit window the world tilted: gray water, gray cloud, Breaker Point’s radio tower blinking like a star trying to remember its name. She counted seconds between flashes—one-Mississippi, two-Mississippi—until the afterimage burned green on her lids.  

She climbed again. At the lantern room the glass had already fogged with her breath. She wiped a circle with her heel of her hand and looked out.  

The ocean’s black mirror showed a woman she barely recognized—hair cropped short and harsh as marsh grass, eyes socketed in shadow, mouth a line drawn by someone no longer in the habit of smiling. Behind the reflection the Atlantic heaved, slow and perpetual, erasing and rewriting itself, older than any promise she had ever made.  

The logbook waited on its shelf, cardboard cover warped by humidity. She opened it, dipped the pen. Ink spread like a bruise across the margin:  

Conditions unremarkable.  

She hesitated, then added: Engine algae moderate. One hatchling found deceased. Wind backing east. Barometer 29.5.  

She paused. The silence in the room was not empty; it was the hush inside seashells, the echo of every wave that had ever struck this rock. She closed the book before it could speak her name.  

Outside, the first fat drop struck the glass with a sound like a finger tapping: let me in. Then another. And another. The Atlantic had finished inhaling; now it exhaled, and the sky opened.  

Mara descended to strike the light before the dark could claim the horizon.

# Echodrift's Bargain

The causeway stones are already slick when Mara steps onto them at half-tide, each granite slab filmed with kelp the color of old bruises. The Atlantic sucks and sighs between the rocks, its breath cold enough to sting inside her nostrils. She tastes diesel before she sees the supply skiff—an oily thread that clings to the back of her throat and will not be swallowed.

Ezra cuts the engine thirty yards out and lets momentum carry him in. The fiberglass hull kisses the platform with a hollow thunk that travels up through Mara's boot-soles and settles in her hipbones. She notices because it is different from Daniel's landing: he always came too fast, throttled back at the last second so the skiff slammed like a thrown shoe. Ezra boats like a man who expects to be billed for damage.

"Morning, keeper." His voice cracks on the second word—not from age but from disuse, forty-odd miles of lonely water between here and the mainland. "Brought your ghost mail."

He tosses a milk crate onto the causeway. Inside: a single manila envelope from the Lighthouse Authority, edges furred by humidity; a plastic jar of powdered creamer the color of bone; two net bags of oranges already greening with mold. The smell rises sweet-rotten, mixing with the low-tide reek of exposed bladderwrack and something deeper, like the inside of a crab shell left too long in sun. Mara's stomach recognizes it before her mind does—their kitchen smelled like this the week after Daniel died, when she could not open the fridge.

Ezra stays in the cockpit, hand resting on the gear lever. She understands: he will not tie off. If the sea stands up while he is ashore, he wants only to shove clear and gun it. The engine idles with an uneven cough that speaks of ethanol-heavy fuel and salt-corroded injectors. Each miss sends a shiver through the water; minnows scatter like silver sparks from a grinding wheel.

"Fuel?" she asks.

"Friday, weather willing." His eyes keep sliding past her to the tower, counting windows maybe, or looking for movement that should not be there. "I'm not saying it's funny, but your transmission last night... sounded like two people talking through one mouth."

Mara's pulse stutters. She has not touched the mic in three days—radio's been nothing but static and the far-off chatter of a tanker plotting course for Halifax. She tastes metal now, sharper than diesel, the way your mouth goes when a filling has cracked.

"Storm interference," she says, because it is easier than asking what voice he heard.

Ezra nods without belief. He shoves the throttle forward an inch; the prop churns up a boil of coffee-colored water that smells of iodine and old pennies. She notices the impeller housing lashed to the stern rail—new, painted the same industrial orange as life vests nobody wears. He notices her noticing.

"Brought one for you too. Backup in case yours gums up again." He pats the housing the way a man pats a dog that might still bite. "Your call, captain."

The words hang between them, carrying more weight than machinery. Mara feels it settle on her collarbones. Last week she pulled a knot of bioluminescent algae from her own intake line—glowing slime that pulsed weakly in her palm like a dying star. She scraped it into the sink and watched it swirl down, still flashing. Now she wonders if that was the first payment on a debt she did not know she owed.

Ezra reverses away, the prop-wash slapping the causeway so hard that spray reaches her shins. The water is August-warm on the surface, cold beneath, the temperature gradient sharp as a lie. She stands there until the skiff becomes a white scar on the horizon, engine noise thinning until it merges with the constant hush of swell against granite.

Alone again, she lifts the crate. The envelope slides, corner rasping across the plastic like a match being struck. She smells the paper before she opens it: mildew and the faint chemical bite of cheap toner. The letterhead is crisp, impersonal.

> Lighthouse Authority – Northeast Sector  
> Contract Amendment 23-B  
> Effective immediately, keepers are reminded that psychological events (defined as hallucinations, unverified auditory phenomena, or persistent feelings of being observed) constitute grounds for relief of duty without severance. Report any such events within 24 hours via secure channel.

The words blur. Not from tears—she is past those—but because the paper is already damp, ink feathering like frost on a window. She hears Daniel's voice then, not memory but present, spoken directly behind her left ear: "They're covering their asses, Skip. Same as always."

Mara does not turn. She has learned not to. Instead she folds the letter into a square small enough to swallow, and tucks it into the hip pocket of her oilskins. The envelope flutters once in the wind, then settles against the crate like a dead gull.

She lifts an orange. The skin gives under her thumb with a soft sigh, releasing a spray of sour-sweet oil that carries, for one impossible second, the scent of Daniel's neck after a day on the water—salt and sunscreen and the lime he used to squeeze into his beer. She closes her fist. Mold squishes between her fingers, warm as living flesh.

The tide is turning. She can feel it in the way the stones begin to vibrate, a low-frequency hum that travels through boot leather and tendon until it nests between her lungs. Soon the causeway will vanish, and the lighthouse will be an island again. She starts back, boots squelching over kelp that has already begun to lift and drift like green flame.

Halfway across she pauses. The air pressure dips—the same sensation she felt the night Daniel left, when the barometer fell so fast it made her ears pop. Out beyond the Cut, the water darkens as if someone has spilled ink across a page. No wind yet, but the gulls have vanished. Their absence rings louder than their cries.

She looks down. Between two stones, water is seeping upward in rhythmic pulses—exactly the cadence of a man breathing through a broken nose. Something glints there: a shard of mussel shell, or maybe the reflection of the lighthouse window in the rising tide. For a heartbeat it looks like an eye, open and watching.

Mara steps over it and does not look back. The tower waits, door ajar, lantern room already beginning to glow as the sun thins behind a shelf of cloud. She smells lamp oil and heated brass, the particular perfume of duty that has outlived every promise made beneath it.

Inside, she sets the crate on the workbench. The oranges roll, one dropping to the floor with a sound like a small skull hitting concrete. She leaves it there, breathing through her mouth so she does not have to taste the rot. When she wipes her hand on a rag, the green mold leaves a trail across the canvas—a phosphorescent smear that catches the faint light from the doorway and holds it, glowing softly, long after the rest of the room has gone dim.

# The Hatchling's Corpse

The lantern room reeked of hot brass and kerosene before Mara struck the first match.  
Dusk bled through salt-fogged panes, turning each into a tarnished mirror that returned four splintered selves: one polishing, one counting, one sleepless, one holding her breath.  
She twisted the wick a thread higher; the threads caught, brass screeching on brass like a memory that refused to smooth.  
A spark leapt, the mantle flared white—too bright to watch straight on—so she followed its reflection: a sun dragged from the sea and caged in crystal.  
Outside, the Atlantic exhaled the day’s heat and inhaled night; the temperature plummeted so fast the iron stairwell pinged as it shrank.  
Somewhere below, a gull screamed—one clean note severed as if by a blade.  

She nudged the lens a quarter-inch clockwise, the way Daniel had when a tanker’s mast kissed the southern bight.  
The counterweight answered with a soft, stubborn clack that climbed the stone and settled in the bones of her feet.  
Every thirty seconds the beam swept, three white ribs carving fog into marble, then letting it collapse back to vapor.  
In the brief glare the causeway gleamed—kelp laid in slick braids, each frond wearing a mercury bead.  
Between flashes the dark rushed in so completely she had to blink to prove the island still existed.  
Glass fogged with her next breath; she scoured an arc with her heel, salt crystals grinding like sand in a wound.  

Downstairs the radio crackled—Ezra’s nightly check, voice frayed by thirty miles of storm-scoured air.  
She let it talk to the static.  
Silence felt safer, as if any syllable might be netted by wind and delivered to whatever listened beyond the Cut.  
She opened the logbook; humidity had warped the cardboard until the corners curled like dried fish skin.  
The pen bled rust against the cream page—same color as the streaks weeping down the tower’s bolts.  
“Conditions unremarkable,” she wrote, the lie settling between the lines.  
Her wrist jumped; a drop spattered, blooming into a black jellyfish that swam halfway across the paper before the fibers drank it dry.  

A low throb rose through the floorboards—diesel engine, maybe two miles out, running dark.  
The vibration entered her soles, climbed her shin bones, nested at the base of her spine.  
She pictured the crew hunched over green radar circles, counting seconds until the shoal ripped their keel like a tin can.  
Three flashes.  
The beam speared a wave crest just as it folded, turning foam to molten glass for the length of a heartbeat.  
In that instant something pale broke the surface—arm-wide, jointless—gone before the lens turned again.  
Her pen hovered, refusing “unverifiable incident,” refusing to let the moment vanish.  

The lantern room began to sweat.  
Condensation pearled on the glass, slid down, pooled on the brass rail where it ate the metal in quiet, patient circles.  
Copper bit the back of her tongue, sharp as the smell after a match struck in a damp cellar.  
Footsteps echoed below—her own, but delayed, as if the tower repeated every motion a half-second late.  
She breathed through her mouth.  
The beam swept; the causeway lay empty now—water, wet stone, and the afterimage of something pale.  
She closed the log, pressed her thumb to the blotter until the skin blanched, then capped the pen with a snap like a bone socketing home.  

Night finished itself while she stood there.  
Stars appeared last, small and remote, their light older than any promise she had ever made.  
She counted them the way Daniel had counted seconds between lightning and thunder—one Mississippi, two—turning distance into time, time into the storm’s true proximity.  
The beam kept its rotation, a metronome for grief, ticking off another thirty seconds of unpaid vigil.  
Somewhere below, the tide climbed the island’s granite thighs, licking higher, tasting what remained.  
Mara stayed at the glass until kerosene scorched her nose raw, until the brass cooled enough to brand her palm, until the next entry felt possible.  
Then she ruled a new line beneath the lie: “Light maintained. Memory persists. Sea unappeased.”

# The Replica on the Causeway

Mara’s boots struck the causeway with the hollow clock of a heart between beats. Fog pressed in, thick as wet wool, erasing the tower behind her and the cottage ahead, leaving only the rock spine and the black inhalation of the Cut thirty feet below. She counted the way she counted everything now—four hundred paces end to end, one hundred twenty-seven iron stairs to the lantern room, twenty-three days left on the contract—numbers that kept grief from spilling over the rim.

The tide was wrong. It hissed through the trench ahead of the chart, slapping stone with a rhythm that felt deliberate. She shifted the coil of spare line on her shoulder and walked faster, right shoulder leading, the same tilt she’d worn since the funeral when the weight stopped being Daniel’s hand and became absence.

A shape waited where the causeway narrowed to three stones’ width. At first she thought it was spray caught in her headlamp, but spray didn’t stand upright or glow with its own faint phosphorus. She halted. The thing thickened—seven feet of moon-bone laced with green-white pulses that slid under the skin like breath beneath thin ice. Its face was almost a man’s, except the lower jaw split in a V, hinges glinting silver where cartilage should be.

It spoke with her mouth.

“One season light for one season return, Skip.”

The nickname cracked her knees worse than the cold. Daniel had dropped half an octave on the word, as if tasting the single malt they couldn’t afford. Hearing it now, flung from an impossible throat, tilted the causeway. She gripped the line to stay upright.

“Not extinguishing anything,” she said. Wind shredded the words. “Find another lighthouse.”

“We did.” The creature cocked its head; inside the translucent skull a slow tide of green rolled front to back, like surf across a submerged window. “Your husband found us. Passage home for passage here. Payment overdue.”

Behind her the tower flashed its thirty-second signature—three white blinks that had steered mariners since Grant was president. Each pulse lit the fog a surgical gray, and in every flash the thing sharpened: collarbone ridges, fingers webbed halfway, nails like chipped quartz. Between flashes only glow and hunger.

Mara’s right hand found the key at her throat. Brass warm from skin, ribbon the color of dried blood. She felt the notches through her glove and wondered, not for the first time, whether the metal held some last residue of Daniel. Three years of salt and polish and she still expected his fingerprint.

“Daniel’s dead,” she said. “Contracts don’t survive the signer.”

“Promises do.” The V flexed; inside, rows of needle teeth angled backward, built to keep what entered. “We kept ours. His boat crossed unbroken. Your light stayed bright. Now you keep his.”

It stepped forward. Water sheeted off its thighs, pattering like rain on stone. The smell rode with it—iodine and diesel laced with something older, the way blood tasted when you bit your tongue at sea. She held her ground, though every tendon thrummed with the urge to run, anywhere that put a solid door between her and this thing.

“You want the light dark,” she said. “Turn it off and ships pile on the shoal. I lose my bonus, maybe my license. Maybe a crew loses their lives. That’s not payment, that’s blackmail.”

“Extinction slower.” Another step. Its feet—long, articulated like a diver’s fins—made no sound on wet rock. “Each hatchling follows your moon to death. We ask navigation. Different map.”

The fog folded inward, erasing the next flash. In the hush she heard her heart, the slap of water, and beneath both a new sound: wet clicking, dozens of plastic spoons knocking. The trench behind the creature boiled with tiny green sparks—hatchlings surfacing, drawn by the argument the way kids gather when parents shout. Their glow was softer, almost pretty until you realized each flicker was a life that would end against steel if the beacon kept calling.

She thought of Owen, nineteen and sharp with contempt only the young can afford. He’d sent every letter back unopened, but the tuition portal still showed zero balance. Anonymous benefactor, the statements read. She pictured him in Portland, maybe studying in a warm library while she bargained with a fish-bright nightmare for the right to keep sending money he didn’t want. The image steadied her.

“No,” she said.

The creature’s glow dimmed, as if the syllable had robbed its lungs of oxygen. For a moment the only light came from the hatchlings below, a green constellation adrift in black water.

Then it smiled—impossible with that jaw, but the corners of its eyes lifted the way Daniel’s had when she tried to refuse him something he knew she’d surrender. It raised one hand. Between webbed fingers dangled a coffee mug, oatmeal glaze chipped at the rim. Daniel’s. She had packed it in the bottom locker last March, wrapped in his wool sweater so the handle wouldn’t break on supply day.

Seeing it suspended over the trench like bait cracked something she’d kept sealed tighter than Owen’s returned envelopes. The fog carried a whimper she didn’t recognize as hers until the creature tilted its head, listening.

“One night,” it said. “One dark night for one true memory. Taste what you guard.”

It set the mug on the stone between them. Inside, two fingers of liquid sloshed—black, steaming though the air was forty degrees. The smell rose: diesel, copper, the ghost of the French roast Daniel used to brew strong enough to etch steel. Her stomach knew it before her brain, clenching around the memory of mornings when the worst danger was whether the bacon would burn.

She knelt without deciding. The key ribbon pulled taut as she leaned forward. One sip, her body bargained, just enough to remember his mouth on the rim. She could almost feel the ceramic warmth, the chip that had scraped his lip the last time—

The lighthouse flashed. In the strobe the mug was only a rusted tin cup filled with seawater that caught the beam like a mirror. She jerked back. The creature’s smile widened, showing the trap: not poison but reflection, a moment so accurate she’d drown trying to hold it.

“Not real,” she whispered.

“Real enough,” it answered. “We keep the shape you made. You keep the light that kills. Choose which memory survives.”

Behind her an engine coughed—Ezra’s supply boat. The creatures heard it; the hatchlings vanished, sparks winking out until only black water remained. The adult straightened, gaze sliding past her toward the unseen boat.

“Time folds,” it said. “We wait below.”

It stepped backward off the causeway. No splash—simply gone, mug and all, as if the trench had opened a door and shut it quietly. Fog rushed into the vacancy, erasing footprints that had never been there.

Mara stayed crouched, lungs heaving like she’d hauled anchor chain by hand. The engine grew louder, then cut, Ezra killing the motor to drift the last fifty yards rather than risk rocks in low visibility. She had maybe three minutes before he saw her shaking and started asking questions that would end with evacuation papers. Three minutes to decide whether to log another unverifiable incident or admit the sea was bargaining for its children.

She stood, wiped spray from her cheeks—tears, maybe, though she couldn’t tell anymore—and walked toward the dock. The key bounced against her sternum with every step, counting down. Twenty-three days. One season. One promise made by a man who hadn’t understood that some debts outlived flesh, glowing in the dark like a lure.

Behind her the tower flashed again, patient, indifferent, bright enough to blind whatever followed it home.
